explain.selection: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial.
explain.answer:
Marcus is rehearsing the day before it starts. He lists the people who will annoy him — the meddler, the ungrateful, the arrogant — so that none of them catches him off guard.

The point comes next: they behave this way because they don't know good from bad, and they are still his kin. Expecting it lets him stay calm instead of angry.

beats.title: Rehearsing the difficult morning
beats.text: Marcus names the busybody, the ungrateful and the envious before he meets them. He disarms them with kinship: they share his reason, so anger at them is one hand fighting the other.

beats.title: A deadline on time
beats.text: He reminds himself that his time is fixed and running out, so each act should be done as if it were his last. Even his beloved books count as distraction here.

beats.title: Only the present moment
beats.text: No one loses any life but the one he is living now, so the longest and shortest lives lose the same. He tests it against three thousand years and finds no difference.

beats.title: Philosophy as the guard
beats.text: Life is short, the body decays and fame is uncertain; only philosophy can guard the spirit within. That means keeping it free of anger, pleasure and pain, and doing nothing at random.
